value.summary: Glaucon and Adeimantus challenge Socrates to defend justice in itself rather than for its extrinsic rewards, prompting Socrates to model justice first in a developing State founded on mutual need and the division of labour.

nodes.label: Threefold Division of Goods
nodes.summary: Glaucon classifies goods into three kinds: those welcomed for their own sake, those desired both for themselves and their results, and burdensome goods desired only for rewards.
nodes.speaker: Glaucon
nodes.rationale: Glaucon sets out an analytic taxonomy distinguishing three classes of desirable things.

nodes.label: Social Contract Origin of Justice
nodes.summary: Glaucon articulates the common view that justice is an agreed compromise between the natural good of committing injustice without penalty and the evil of suffering injustice without redress.
nodes.speaker: Glaucon
nodes.rationale: Organizes the conventional theory explaining why laws and standards of justice are created and upheld.

nodes.label: Ring of Gyges Thought Experiment
nodes.summary: Glaucon recounts the tale of Gyges using an invisibility ring to seize power, arguing that anyone freed from fear of discovery would act unjustly.
nodes.speaker: Glaucon
nodes.rationale: A concrete narrative illustration demonstrating that men practice justice only involuntarily.

nodes.label: Praise of Justice for External Gain
nodes.summary: Adeimantus argues that parents, poets, and prose writers praise justice merely for reputation, social advancement, and divine favour, rather than its intrinsic worth.
nodes.speaker: Adeimantus
nodes.rationale: A broad critical overview of cultural, poetic, and religious rhetoric surrounding justice and divine propitiation.

nodes.label: The Demand to Defend Justice Itself
nodes.identityLabel: defence of justice in the soul
nodes.summary: Adeimantus challenges Socrates to demonstrate what justice and injustice accomplish on their own inside the soul, stripped of external reputations and rewards.
nodes.speaker: Adeimantus
nodes.rationale: Defines the fundamental organizing question and mandate that governs the rest of the dialogue.

nodes.label: State Analogy: The Large Letters
nodes.summary: Socrates proposes to locate justice by examining a State first, likening it to reading large letters before examining smaller ones in the individual.
nodes.speaker: Socrates
nodes.rationale: Establishes the macro-level interpretive framework used to investigate justice in the soul.

nodes.label: Foundation of the State on Human Need
nodes.summary: Socrates states that a city originates because individuals are not self-sufficing but have numerous bodily and material needs that require mutual cooperation.
nodes.speaker: Socrates
nodes.rationale: A core premise detailing the fundamental cause of social organization.

nodes.label: Specialization and Division of Labour
nodes.summary: Socrates and Adeimantus deduce that work is better and more plentiful when each citizen performs the single craft fitted to their natural disposition.
nodes.speaker: Socrates
nodes.rationale: A reusable organizing economic principle governing the construction of the ideal city.

edges.rationale: The thought experiment of Gyges' ring demonstrates Glaucon's claim that justice is only practiced of necessity and not willingly.
Adeimantus's review of how poets and teachers praise only the consequences of justice grounds his requirement that Socrates defend justice in itself.
The large-letters method of examining justice in the city is introduced as Socrates' direct procedural response to the brothers' challenge.
The construction of the city based on basic human wants carries out the proposal to trace justice in a State.
The division of labour specifies how the newly formed community effectively satisfies the multiple needs that brought it into being.
